title: Why a rocket that learned to fly could not learn to hover
paper_title: RocketSim: Benchmarking Reinforcement-Learning Hover Control of a Reusable Booster
date_note: Information Society 2026 multiconference, Ljubljana, early October 2026 (proceedings Vol. 1, pp. 64-67); exact day approximate
authors: Swarnendu Ghosh, David Muhič, Branko Šter
summary: A short guide to the RocketSim paper: a learning agent kept a booster upright but could not hold its height, and why. The full write-up is on the LANCER project page.
cta: Read the full write-up on the LANCER page

body.p: This paper is part of LANCER, my postdoctoral project at the University of Ljubljana on teaching autonomous vehicles to navigate difficult environments with reinforcement learning, which is learning by trial and error against a reward. This paper steps sideways to a rocket booster and asks what happens when the learner has no clear goal event.

Earlier learning-based work on reusable rockets targets landing, where touchdown gives the learner a clear goal. We asked about hovering instead: release a booster at 80 metres and ask it to hold 30 metres above the pad. We built a simulator called RocketSim in the Unity game engine and trained an agent with PPO, a standard algorithm.

figure.alt: Five test flights of one trained agent: the plan views show tight lateral control while the altitude traces sag below the 30 metre target, approach the ground, then climb to the ceiling.
figure.caption: Five test flights of one trained agent. It stays over the pad, but its height sags below the target, nears the ground, then climbs to the ceiling.

body.p: The agent learned to stay upright, stay over the pad and fly until its tanks ran dry, but not to hold the commanded height. With nothing changed but the random seed, its final altitude ranged from the ground to the ceiling. Across five seeds the score varied by less than ±10%, yet the mean altitude error ranged from 24 to 105 metres. Repeated runs used a faster, simplified version of the task.

There are two causes. Far from the target the reward barely changes with height, so PPO has no gradient to follow, although a hand-written controller that obeys the command scores 23% more. And below 33.6 tonnes the engine cannot throttle under its 39% floor, so for the last 55% of the burn no setting holds altitude.

We tried to repair both. Three reshaped objectives cut the mean final error from 36 to 6 metres but still strand one seed in five, and a vehicle that can throttle down sinks instead. Hover has to be fixed in the reward and in the vehicle together. RocketSim is uncalibrated against flight data, so it is an algorithmic simulation, not a trajectory predictor. The project page has the rest.
